title: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers
summary: This article provides a comprehensive guide on training and finetuning multi-vector embedding models using the Sentence Transformers library. It introduces the MultiVectorEncoder model type, explains the benefits of finetuning for domain-specific retrieval tasks, and details the components involved in the training process, including models, datasets, loss functions, and training arguments. The post includes practical examples, performance evaluations, and recommendations for starting points and configurations to optimize retrieval performance.
key_points: Sentence Transformers v6.0 introduces MultiVectorEncoder for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, enabling token-level matching for improved retrieval performance.

Finetuning multi-vector models significantly enhances retrieval performance for domain-specific tasks (e.g., medical, legal, or code search) by preserving fine-grained signals lost in single-vector models.
Multi-vector models outperform general-purpose retrievers, especially for long documents, as they avoid truncation issues common in dense models.

Training components include the model (existing or built from scratch), datasets, loss functions (e.g., CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss), training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class.

Starting points for training matter: unsupervised checkpoints adapt better to new domains than fully finetuned models, and fresh projections on strong backbones (e.g., ModernBERT) are effective alternatives.
Datasets can be sourced from the Hugging Face Hub or local files, with formats tailored to the chosen loss function (e.g., query-passage pairs for in-batch negatives training).
Key training arguments include batch size, learning rate, precision (FP16/BF16), and prompts for query/document markers. GradCache enables larger effective batch sizes without memory spikes.
Evaluation shows that finetuned multi-vector models (e.g., mLateOn-medical) outperform dense, sparse, and lexical models on domain-specific benchmarks like medical retrieval.
Practical optimizations include adjusting document length limits, using punctuation skiplists to reduce index size, and avoiding scale saturation in loss functions.
